passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you for standing by. Good day, everyone, and welcome to the Amazon.com Q3 2026 Financial Results Teleconference. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the presentation, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. Today's call is being recorded. For opening remarks, I'll be turning the call over to the Vice President of Investor Relations, Mr. Dave Fildes. Thank you, sir. Please go ahead.

passages.heading: Dave Fildes, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: Dave Fildes, Vice President of Investor Relations: Hello, and welcome to our Q3 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. Joining us today to answer your questions is Andy Jassy, our CEO, and Brian Olsavsky, our CFO. As you listen to today's conference call, we encourage you to have our press release in front of you, which includes our financial results, as well as metrics and commentary on the quarter. Please note, unless otherwise stated, all comparisons in this call will be against our results for the comparable period of 2025. Our comments and responses to your questions reflect management's views as of today, October 29, 2026, only, and will include forward-looking statements. Actual results may differ materially. Additional information about factors that could potentially impact our financial results is included in today's press release and our filings with the SEC, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K and subsequent filings. During this call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures. In our press release, slides accompanying this webcast, and our filings with the SEC, each of which is posted on our IR website, you will find additional disclosures regarding these non-GAAP measures, including reconciliations of these measures with comparable GAAP measures. Our guidance incorporates the order trends that we've seen to date and what we believe today to be appropriate assumptions. Our results are inherently unpredictable and may be materially

passages.heading: Dave Fildes, Vice President of Investor Relations
passages.text: affected by many factors, including fluctuations in foreign exchange rates and energy prices, changes in global economic and geopolitical conditions, tariff and trade policies, resource and supply volatility, including for memory chips, and customer demand and spending, including the impact of recessionary fears, inflation, interest rates, regional labor market constraints, world events, the rate of growth of the internet, online commerce, cloud services, and new and emerging technologies, and the various factors detailed in our filings with the SEC. Our guidance assumes, among other things, that we don't conclude any additional business acquisitions, restructurings, or legal settlements. It's not possible to accurately predict demand for our goods and services, and therefore, our actual results could differ materially from our guidance. I'll turn the call over to Andy.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: Thanks, Dave. We're reporting $201.9 billion in revenue, up 12% year-over-year. Operating income was $28.1 billion, up 61% year-over-year. Q3 was another strong quarter for Amazon. In AWS, our plan is working. Despite lapping a comparable year-over-year period where we added a lot of capacity, AWS grew 39.3% year-over-year, accelerating for the sixth straight quarter, our fastest growth in nearly five years. Backlog is $578 billion, growing triple digits year-over-year and well-diversified. We're installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up. Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years. Our operating margins have long been strong on our core offering, but are rapidly improving on the AI side too, well ahead of where they were on core at a similar time of evolution, even with heightened component costs like memory and significant depreciation from the CapEx we're investing. We continue to accelerate our CapEx payback and have even more conviction than we already had that the investment we're making in AWS will yield a much larger revenue- and free-cash-flow-generating business than we would have imagined a couple of years ago, with strong return on invested capital. We have a compelling flywheel spinning in AWS. Borrowing from Jim Collins' flywheel definition in "Good to Great," where if you do A, you almost can't help but do B, and if you do

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: B, you almost can't help but do C, and so on. In AWS, having the leading functionality, security, and operational performance can't help but drive customers to run their apps and store their data in AWS, which can't help but drive AWS AI demand because customers prefer their production inference to be near the rest of their data and apps, which can't help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, post-training, and tool usage, which can't help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality. This is a different model than primarily hosting GPUs or renting short-term data center capacity. This is a long-term platform strategy that broadly helps customers invent and evolve their customer experiences, operate stably, and build a reliable partnership they can grow for many years. It also yields very attractive long-term economics for us, regardless of supply scarcity. There are many examples that illustrate our progress in AWS, but I'll share a few. On the core side, it's important to remember that the vast majority of global IT spend, about 85%, is still on premises, and we're in a 10- to 20-year cycle where that equation will flip to the cloud. Conventional wisdom has been that linchpin workloads like mainframes or storage area networks would never move to the cloud, but these workloads are moving as AWS has built unique cloud substitutes and AI-driven migration capabilities to make this transition much easier.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Enterprises get the benefits of less CapEx, lower operating costs, faster innovation, better developer productivity, and data accessibility to more easily leverage AI. Our core business has attractive margins because we've learned to run it very efficiently over the last 20 years. As our core business grows, we keep reinvesting in our core and AI functionality. For example, as customers generate increasingly more data and seek to get value from it in analytics and AI, the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines is onerous and expensive. With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS Storage and Analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use, and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service. For the first time in analytics, customers will have zero migration or portability costs between query engines. This is a big deal, and you can imagine how it will also help agents do efficient querying as well. On the AI side, we continue to expand the capabilities of our inference service, Amazon Bedrock, and it is leading to remarkable growth, with Fortune 500 companies spending nearly 7x more on Bedrock year-over-year and total Bedrock token volume growing nearly 17x year-over-year. Bedrock is the fastest-growing multi-billion-dollar service in AWS's history. We have recently added OpenAI

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: models to Bedrock, and usage is growing quickly. We also just added Bedrock-managed versions of Kimi, GLM, and SpaceX models. You cannot have a conversation about AI today without talking about security, and it is another reason customers keep choosing Bedrock. We have designed Bedrock so customers' data remains secure and private. Inputs and outputs are never shared with model providers or used to train base models. When customers tune a foundation model, we create a private copy specifically for their use, and data is fully encrypted both in transit and at rest. As frontier models get more powerful, they are surfacing software vulnerabilities previously not found and at unprecedented rates. We built AWS Continuum to discover, prioritize, validate, and remediate code vulnerabilities at machine speed. It is already being used by customers like Capital One, IBM, Infor, Luminate, and Robinhood. In Q3, we announced that we will integrate it into the tools where code is being written: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, and AWS's Kiro. The interest from customers exceeds anything we have ever seen for a new security service. Agents continue to be deployed at accelerating rates, many of which are being built on AgentCore's building blocks. Tens of thousands of customers currently use AgentCore, deploying 2x more agents with it in Q3 than the prior three quarters combined. In addition to building their own purpose-built agents, most companies will also use turnkey agentic

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: services, and we offer several that customers love: Kiro for coding, Amazon Connect for contact center agents, and AWS Transform for migrations. They are all iterating quickly and picking up customer momentum. As is Amazon Quick, our intelligent AI work companion, which is growing very rapidly as large enterprises like Mondelez, EchoStar, 3M, Southwest Airlines, and DXC Technology are choosing Quick because it is purpose-built for work with no compromises on customer data. Finally, our chips business continues to grow triple-digit percentages year-over-year, and revenue commitments for Graviton and Trainium have each increased more than 20x year-over-year. AI continues to be a tailwind for Graviton because post-training reinforcement learning and agent tool use is mostly done on CPUs versus AI accelerators, and Graviton is the strongest CPU chip, offering up to 30%-40% better price performance than alternatives. Customers using our custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone, and we just open-sourced TorchNeuron so developers can run existing PyTorch code, which most already use, on Trainium without rewriting a thing. As we launch new generations of chips, demand for prior generations remains strong. After our launch of Graviton5, backlog for prior-generation Graviton instances still more than doubled quarter-over-quarter. Short-term capacity for prior-generation Trainium instances sells at a premium compared to the first half of the year. With Trainium demand so

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027. Overall demand for AWS capacity remains exceptionally strong. Enterprises are still very early in using inference at scale, and yet inference already accounts for well over half of AWS's AI revenue and is growing, and we have a lot of training revenue as well. We still expect 2026 cash CapEx of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027 with a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns, as I laid out on our last call. AWS is a $184 billion annualized revenue run-rate business, and yet the opportunity remains extraordinary. With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we're adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years. We're in the very early days of this inflection. Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future. In stores, I think some folks are sleeping a bit on how much progress that business has made and what it's become over the last few years. I'm not aware of another retail business approaching Amazon's revenue size, hundreds of billions of dollars, with double-digit operating margins inclusive of ads that's growing at this pace. Year to date,

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: units have grown nearly 15% year-over-year, and that's on an enormous base, having sold more than 30 billion items last year. In absolute dollar terms, we've added more than $90 billion in gross sales in the trailing 12 months, and we're growing meaningfully faster than other retail competitors, adding about double the gross sales per quarter than our next-largest competitor in the U.S. and consistently taking retail market segment share. Over the past few years, our North America and International segments have each expanded operating margins by nearly 10 percentage points, which enables us to reinvest in making the customer experience even better. Remember, it's still early. The significant majority of retail, nearly 80%, currently occurs in physical stores. That will eventually flip to e-commerce over time. We're helping enable this shift by rapidly building out our efficient and speedy fulfillment network, providing delightful customer experiences while driving significant free cash flow and return on invested capital. Each of our priorities, from faster delivery, to cost to serve, to groceries and pharmacy, to AI shopping, are force multipliers, and we're firing on all cylinders. Our delivery speeds keep getting faster as we invest in our same-day network, as well as our Amazon Now and Amazon Prime Air ultrafast services. We had our fastest Q3 ever globally, and we delivered more than 1.5 billion items to Prime customers same day or overnight in Q3. We're energized by

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: the customer response to our rapid rollout of Amazon Now around the world. It's now available in over 450 towns and cities, and the number of items ordered through Amazon Now is up 10x year-over-year. We're on track to reduce cost to serve per unit for the fourth consecutive year, which enables us to continue meeting or beating competitors' prices, and cost-effectively deliver a broad selection of fresh groceries and Everyday Essentials. Increasing speed is fueling our grocery business, including perishables and Everyday Essentials, and gross sales grew to nearly $250 billion in the trailing 12 months. In Q3, fresh groceries and Everyday Essentials grew about three times faster than the rest of our store, representing about half of all units sold. Customers who shop perishables with same-day delivery buy nearly seven times more Everyday Essential units than those who don't. Active grocery customers shop nearly four times more non-grocery categories like home and apparel, and spend over two times more on those categories compared to non-grocery customers. Amazon Pharmacy is also growing fast. The number of customers using it is up over 60% year-over-year, with growth accelerating each quarter through 2026. Repeat customers grew more than 50% year-over-year. J.D. Power recently ranked Amazon Pharmacy the top mail-order pharmacy for the third year in a row, and we keep making it even better, now offering three-hour prescription delivery in more than 350 cities. Over 400

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: million customers have used Alexa for Shopping, our agentic shopping assistant, in the last 12 months, with customer interactions up 570% year-over-year. U.S. customers using Alexa for Shopping are spending 50% more per order than those who don't. It researches products, compares options, checks a full year of price history, gets personalized gift recommendations, and tracks deals and price drops on customers' behalf. Though we anticipate working with horizontal agents, we believe Alexa for Shopping is going to be the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon. Having a shopping assistant constantly by your side as you browse, get inspired, have questions on product detail pages, and that you can simply ask to buy something based on your prior purchases that already have your history, your shipping address, and payment info, is uniquely helpful and convenient for customers. Moving to Amazon Ads, we generated $19.6 billion of revenue in Q3, up 12% year-over-year. Though there were some timing anomalies in this past quarter, we continue to be pleased with the overall momentum across our ad offerings. I'll mention three items impacting the growth rates. First, we shifted Prime Day into Q2 for most countries, moving significant sales and ad revenue that were in Q3 2025 into Q2 2026, a tailwind to our Q2 2026 rate and a headwind to Q3 2026. For advertising, that was an 850-basis-point sequential impact to Q3 year-over-year growth. Second, Q2 2026 included the first

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: season of NBA on Prime, which last year's Q2 didn't have. Q3 does not include any NBA; it starts in Q4. Third, in Q3 2025, we changed our search engine marketing programs to drive more traffic to search pages on Amazon. It's a better experience for customers, and we also monetize that traffic at a higher rate. That helped accelerate advertising revenue growth starting a year ago, and we started lapping that in Q3. We expect year-over-year growth will return to the high teens in Q4. The natural question is whether agentic shopping from external horizontal agents is meaningfully impacting Amazon Ads. The answer is no. Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet, as the experience is still not great nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly to research or one-click order there. Q3 was chock-full of innovation from our ads team that we expect to have impact in the coming months, headlined by Amazon Ads Agent, which brings together our full advertising offering under a single AI-first platform. Backed by trillions of shopping, browsing, and streaming signals, it supports advertisers at every step with insights, answers, and the ability to optimize and act on their behalf. We also launched full-funnel campaigns in Amazon Ads Agent, bringing sponsored ads, display, video, and streaming TV into a single campaign. Advertisers provide initial inputs, including budget and duration, and Amazon's AI plans, executes, and continually optimizes the rest. We're

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: continuing to see momentum in several other areas. I'll mention just a few. Prime Video has emerged as a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars, now profitable in its own right. We have momentum with hit shows like Carrie, The Summer I Turned Pretty, The Boys, Off Campus, Reacher, and Fallout. Breakout movies like Project Hail Mary, along with compelling live sports, including Thursday Night Football, off to its best start ever in 2026, NBA on Prime, NASCAR, the Masters, and UEFA Champions League soccer. We recently launched our most powerful devices lineup yet with 34 new products across Echo, Kindle, Alexa tablets, Fire TV, Ring, and Bee. It's early, but we're off to a very strong start and excited for more customers to get their hands on these as we head into the holidays. Finally, Amazon Leo remains on track to begin initial service this year. We're heading into one of our most exciting stretches of the year with both re:Invent and the holidays. I want to thank our teammates for their hard work and invention to make customers' lives better and easier every day. What we're building at Amazon is unlike anything that's ever been seen before. There has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue. Amazon is on a path to have two of them in AWS and stores. It's rare, and we're energized by what's ahead. Over to you, Brian.

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: Brian Olsavsky, CFO: Thank you, Andy. Let's start with our top-line financial results. Worldwide revenue was $201.9 billion, a 12% increase year-over-year, and a 13% increase year-over-year excluding the impact of foreign exchange. Worldwide operating income was $28.1 billion, with an operating margin of 13.9%, which is our highest operating margin ever. Starting with our North America and International segments results. First, let me remind you that Prime Day shifted this year, with the sales event occurring in Q2 for most of our largest countries, including the U.S. In 2025, Prime Day was entirely in Q3. Excluding the impact of this Prime Day time change, the third quarter 2026 year-over-year growth would be approximately 400 basis points higher. In Q3, we saw strong customer engagement and a continuation of trends from the first half of the year. In the North America segment, third quarter revenue was $112.9 billion, an increase of 6% year-over-year. International segment revenue was $43.1 billion, an increase of 8% year-over-year, excluding the impact of foreign exchange. Worldwide paid units grew 12% year-over-year. Prime remains a key pillar of our business. Hundreds of millions of Prime members are responding to our combination of vast selection, low prices, and record delivery speeds. Over the past year, monthly orders of fresh groceries placed by our Prime members for free same-day delivery have more than tripled. Let's shift to profitability. North America segment

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: operating income was $8.7 billion, with an operating margin of 7.7%. International segment operating income was $1.6 billion, with an operating margin of 3.7%. In our fulfillment network, the team navigated higher transportation costs from fuel inflation and higher line-haul rates. Even with these headwinds, we still lowered our overall cost to serve in Q3 through better inventory placement, shorter shipping distances, and package consolidation. Shipping costs increased 11% year-over-year versus a 12% increase in units. Excluding fuel and line-haul inflation, shipping costs grew 8%, or approximately 400 basis points slower than unit growth. Robotics and AI are delivering measurable gains through productivity and employee safety, which we expect to compound in the future. In 2026, we doubled our fleet of robotic arms like Cardinal and Sparrow. We're also developing robotics foundation models that enable faster programming and teach robots increasingly complex physical tasks, with the goal of delivering useful robotics at scale. Looking ahead, we see meaningful opportunities to improve productivity across our global fulfillment network and lower our cost to serve while continuing to get products to customers faster. Our operating margin may fluctuate quarter-to-quarter, but we're focused on sustained long-term improvement in our cost to serve per unit. Moving to our AWS segment, revenue was $46 billion and grew 39.3% year-over-year, driven by both core and AI services. We

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: added $3.8 billion in quarter-over-quarter revenue. AWS now has an annualized revenue run rate of $184 billion. Customers continue to move to the cloud and scale their use of AWS core services, and increasingly, customers who want the full benefits of AI are accelerating their transition to the cloud. We see a strong linkage between AI spend and growth in our revenue for core services. As customers invest in AI, we see a corresponding increase in core consumption, and we expect that relationship to strengthen as more AI workloads move into production and drive additional demand for compute, storage, and networking. AWS operating income was $17.8 billion, with an operating margin of 38.7%, reflecting strong growth and our focus on driving efficiencies. Our investments in custom chips and custom networking, along with software and process improvements, are helping us optimize capacity and build a more cost-efficient infrastructure. As we've long said, we expect AWS operating margins to fluctuate, driven in part by the level of investment we're making at any point in time. Our AI offerings are gaining traction with customers, with AI revenue growing triple digits year-over-year. Bedrock has been a significant growth driver. Turning to our cash CapEx, which was $75.9 billion in Q3. This primarily relates to AWS and AI as we invest to support strong customer demand. We continue to make significant investments, especially in AI, as we believe it to be a massive opportunity with

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: the potential to drive long-term revenue and free cash flow, as well as return on invested capital. I'll finish with our financial guidance for Q4. Q4 net sales are expected to be between $240 billion and $247 billion. We estimate the year-over-year impact of changes in foreign exchange rates based on current rates, which we expect to be a headwind of approximately 60 basis points in the quarter. Q4 operating income is expected to be between $28.5 billion and $33.5 billion. I'll mention one factor impacting our Q4 guidance. Amazon Leo's commercial service is on track to begin initial service this year, and we expect to begin capitalizing certain costs in Q1 of next year, including production and launch costs. This is later than I've been predicting in earlier earnings calls. As a result, we will continue to expense the majority of Leo-related costs in Q4. We're ready to serve customers this holiday season and to support the millions of customers building with AWS.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: I want to thank our teams across Amazon for their hard work and focus on customers. Our commitment to elevating the customer experience remains the only reliable way to create lasting value for our shareholders. With that, let's move on to your questions.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. At this time, we will now open the call up for questions. We ask each caller to please limit yourself to one question. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your keypad. We ask that when you pose your question, you pick up your handset to provide optimum sound quality. Once again, to initiate a question, please press star, then one on your touch-tone telephone at this time. Please hold while we poll for questions. Thank you. Our first question comes from the line of Justin Post with Bank of America. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Justin Post, Analyst
passages.text: Justin Post, Analyst: Great. Thank you. Andy, we continue to see the cloud business accelerate, which is really nice, but the quarter-over-quarter growth slowed. I am just wondering if there are any call-outs there on the customer side or token costs or anything that kind of drove that, and how you are thinking about the capacity adds in Q4. Brian, maybe just any impact of fuel costs on your guidance in Q4. Thank you.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: I will start with the growth question. We are really pleased with the growth. 39.3% on a business that has got a $184 billion annual revenue run rate is quite unusual. Our fastest growth in about five years, or six quarters consecutively of acceleration. We are adding quite a bit of capacity. I think if you look at what is driving the growth right now, it is a combination of a few things. First, on the AI side, the unusual top-to-bottom stack functionality we have, whether you are building your own model with SageMaker AI, which is the easiest way to build your own model, or you want to leverage one of the leading frontier models with high security and very strong price performance, people can use Bedrock. Whether you are building your own agents, where we have capabilities like Strands and AgentCore to build and to run those securely and scalably, or you are going to use turnkey agents, which most companies do. If you just look across, Kiro for coding and Amazon Connect for call center and AWS Transform for migrations and Amazon Quick, which is growing incredibly fast as an AI companion at work. People are adopting those very quickly. We add a lot of capacity every quarter. The amount that we add every quarter is not equal. We are adding different amounts each quarter. If I look at how much we have added this year and what we have planned over the next, I will call it, eight quarters or so, which is about as far out as we get—eight to 10 quarters—we have a

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: lot of capacity coming as well. Then, I layer on top of that too, just the impact of chips. We're very well positioned for what's happening in AI because increasingly, what you're finding right now is most customers, every customer that uses AI at scale, but particularly enterprises now as they're starting to deploy more inference into production, are very eager to save on price performance. Trainium, with the meaningful advantage it has in price performance versus other alternatives, is very compelling to people. Then as more and more people are using AI in a very broad way, it drives a lot of the core in capabilities like reinforcement learning and post-training and tool calling. We have the leading CPU chip in Graviton, which is about 30%-40% more price performant than the other x86 providers. So those things are really driving very significant growth. The amount of capacity we add each quarter will vary, but at this scale to be projecting growth of over 40% year-over-year in each of 2027 and 2028 is pretty significant. And the fact that we believe that this can be a trillion-dollar revenue business in five to 10 years—it's an extraordinary, unusual opportunity that we're very excited to be pursuing.

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: Brian Olsavsky, CFO: Justin, on your question about fuel and line-haul inflation, I would say I don't have an exact number for you, but it is higher in Q4 than it was in Q3. If you remember, we instituted a fuel surcharge at the beginning of the year for FBA sellers that recovers some, but not all, of the costs that we're seeing on fuel for those shipments. Then the remaining part is on the retail inbound shipments and outbound shipments. So it's in there. It's a little bit higher than Q3.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Brian Nowak with Morgan Stanley. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Brian Nowak, Analyst
passages.text: Brian Nowak, Analyst: Thanks for taking my questions. I have two. Andy, your excitement about AWS is coming through the line, and it is pretty rare you would make comments about a trillion dollars of revenue five to 10 years from now. It is more than you usually give. Can you just maybe walk us through how you get to that trillion dollars? Is it top-down? Is it bottom-up? What gives you confidence that you are going to be able to put up that type of revenue growth and to get to that type of a number in the next five to 10 years? The second one, just for either of you: On the robotics side, as we look into 2027, what are the key milestones you are both focused on for the Retail business?

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: Yeah. On the AWS side, if you just look at the growth rates, Brian, look at the growth rates on the run rate, and then look at what we are projecting in 2027 and 2028. As I have said a few times, we will always, despite how much capacity we are providing, have big chunks of capacity that people take—the hundreds of megawatts or sometimes up to a gigawatt of capacity. Those big chunks are reserved well in advance because you cannot leave a gigawatt of capacity hanging around. We have very good visibility into 2027 and 2028 and some of 2029 too, with respect to what customers want in those really big chunks of capacity. We will always leave a fair bit of capacity available for on-demand, on EC2 or in Bedrock, and we are working closely with our customers, and they will have plenty of capacity to be able to use in AWS. We have very good visibility into the next few years on what AWS looks like. Those types of growth rates, when you do the math on the revenue and the revenue run rate we have, get you pretty quickly to escalating numbers. I would say that on top of not believing that a lot of the usage we see today is going to attenuate anytime soon, we are still really early in enterprises using inference in their production applications in a pervasive way. It is just really early, and some of that is enterprises having enough people who know how to operate an AI and post-train and fine-tune models for the right applications. Some of it is the cost of inference.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: I think if we all want enterprises to be able to use inference the way we all believe they will, we have to keep working on taking the cost of inference down. That is a huge mission for AWS. It's one of the significant reasons why we're building our own custom silicon in Trainium, is that we just really believe it's incredibly important for customers to be able to use inference in a much more cost-effective way. That has come down a lot, the cost of inference, over the last couple of years, and I think it will come down meaningfully more. Then you just think about what you're seeing. If you think about security as an example, just by itself, the models today are so advanced that the vulnerabilities that they're finding, humans just haven't found. If you've had access to these models, you're using these models to both find them and ultimately to help with patching them and deploying, and there are some people who think that the total amount of tokens used over the next year or two—20% of it is some significant percent of it may end up being just security. That's a relatively new use case on top of what we're seeing with coding and how that continues to grow, on top of what we're seeing with the various, I'll call it, AI companions, both in the consumer space and in the workspace, like with Quick. These are just the initial big use cases. You layer on top of that what you're going to see with enterprises, where I believe virtually every modern enterprise production

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: application will be rewritten to be agentically capable, because that's the way you're going to have to deploy if you want to move quickly or you want to actually guard in the right way against some of the security risks. There is just so much AI coming. You can't predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates, but it's not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion-dollar business. On the robotics side, what I would say is that it's pretty remarkable what's happening in robotics right now. I'll say in general, but particularly at Amazon. We have over 1 million robots now in our fulfillment network, and while they're having very significant impact on our cost structure and on our productivity and on safety, if you look at our safety numbers in our fulfillment network, they're at record-low numbers. We've made huge progress over the last four to five years, and robotics has been a big piece of that. Yet, I would tell you we're still so early with respect to both what we have built and deployed and what we're working on. I think that you'll see, we will always have a lot of teammates in our fulfillment centers. But I think a lot of the jobs that we have that are more repetitive that we have humans doing will be done by robots. I think we're investing in all sorts of additional robotics of all different form factors. I think we have the opportunity to also assist on some of the delivering of the last 100

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: yards to customer doors. We have a lot coming, and for us, the way we measure robotics is: Does it lead to comparable or better productivity, safety, cost structure, and time to delivery? When we like that combination of economics, we will deploy it at scale in our fulfillment network. If I look at the new designs that we have coming in our fulfillment network, including our expansion of same-day facilities, they are very heavy on robotics. We think it has had a big impact, and we think it is small compared to what it is going to be in the next five years.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Mark Mahaney with Evercore ISI. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Mark Mahaney, Analyst
passages.text: Mark Mahaney, Analyst: Two things. First, thanks a lot for the forward comments on AWS growth. Could I ask you to draw out on margins too? I know that margins can move up and down quarter-to-quarter, but over the next two years, do you think the current margin structure is relatively stable? Do we kind of hold at these high-30%, 40% operating margins for AWS? On perishable checkout, I am super excited about this opportunity, just watching how it has rolled out in my neighborhood and in other areas. How much coverage do you have for perishable checkout? In other words, how many Prime households do you think you have covered with perishable checkout? For those that have used it, how much of a boost do you think that is per Prime household? Is this something that increases spend per Prime household by 20%, 50%, 100%, just given how large the fresh grocery category is? Thanks a lot.

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: Brian Olsavsky, CFO: Hey, Mark, let me start with the operating margin outlook for AWS. We are not guiding at all on our margin for AWS, but I can give you my color on it. It seems very strong: operating margin was 38.7% this quarter. I would add that the profitability you have been seeing recently is not a random output. It is the result of a lot of disciplined efficiency gains, capacity optimization, closely managing our fixed cost, and, as Andy said, the inclusion, over time, of more and more custom chips into our cost structure. However, there are other things bouncing around. In fact, the outsized growth of AI puts margin pressure on the business as a whole because the margins are lower there. We are happy with the progression in both core and AI margins, and as Andy said earlier, they are ahead of where the core was at a similar point in time, but they are still lower, so there is going to be that mix issue. There are also headwinds from component pricing that we have talked about. We cannot predict it, but there is going to be always a confluence of these multiple factors that we are working very hard on the cost side and the efficiency side in dealing with investments and new product margins as they start up and launch and reach scale. On the perishables checkout, Mark, I share your enthusiasm about it. As you know, we have had a big grocery business for a while, and it has mostly been in the middle aisles of what you would find in a grocery store: consumables,

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: canned goods, pharmaceutical items, beauty products. We have had this leading organic grocery store in Whole Foods Market, which also is growing faster than the rest of the grocery segment, both in the top line and the bottom line, with a new format and Daily Shop in urban environments. It is doing really well, and we are in the process of rolling it out over the next couple of years. We have always known if we wanted to be able to serve customers the way we think they want to be served and the way we want to, we have to have a mass offering, and it starts with perishables. And if you look at the total spend per household, when we look at the difference between the total amount of spend that we think our consumers and customers are spending on items that we could serve them on versus what they spend with us, the biggest difference is grocery. In a lot of your shops, a lot of grocery starts with perishables, and so we really are excited that we feel like we found something with shipping perishables out of our same-day facilities. We have grown our Everyday Essentials about three times faster than the rest of our store. It represents about half of our units now, if I look at all the Everyday Essentials. What we find is customers who shop perishables through our same-day delivery, they buy about seven times more Everyday Essential units than those that do not. Again, if you are trying to close that gap between what consumers spend overall on the items that we can provide

passages.heading: Brian Olsavsky, CFO
passages.text: versus what they spend with us, perishables has a huge impact on that. We also see that our grocery customers shop about four times more non-grocery categories, like home and apparel and a bunch of other categories, and spend about two times more on those categories compared to those who do not use us for grocery. Those are big differences, and we believe that the progress we are making on perishables and grocery is going to ultimately lead to being more relevant to customers for more of their shopping missions.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Eric Sheridan with Goldman Sachs. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Eric Sheridan, Analyst
passages.text: Eric Sheridan, Analyst: Thanks so much for taking the question. Maybe a two-parter on market opportunities within AWS. First, with respect to Bedrock, what have been your key learnings about the market opportunity around Bedrock and how it might continue to scale in the years ahead? Then with respect to the decision to sell Trainium externally, how do you think about balancing the market opportunity of external sales relative to the need for compute for that opportunity relative to other opportunities broadly across both internal use cases and AWS? Thanks so much.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: Yeah. On the Bedrock side, I would tell you you've probably heard this from us multiple times over the last couple of years, but one of the lessons that we've learned, I'll say for 20-plus years in offering technology to customers, is that there is not one tool to rule the world. People always assume that whatever is in the lead early on is going to be the only thing or things that people use, and it's never the case. It's not true in database, it hasn't been true in analytics. In the beginning of AI, everyone said the only framework people use is TensorFlow. It turns out PyTorch is much bigger now. It's not going to be true with models either. I'll say in the next two to three years, I think there are going to be six to eight models that are about as good as each other, or at least good enough for 95%+ of the workloads. Some will be better at reasoning, some will be better at coding, some will be better at visual pieces, some will be lower latency, and some will be lower cost. Most customers are going to use multiple models, and many will use multiple models in the same generative AI application. What customers really want to do, and we see this validated over and over again when we talk to customers, is they want a service that has really broad selection of those frontier models, and that has very good price performance, and that has very strong security and access control. They want that service so that they can decide what combination of models they want

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: to use and to swap them back and forth as they leapfrog each other, as different constraints of their applications require them. That's what we see with Bedrock. People are very excited about it. We have both closed models and models like Anthropic and OpenAI's models. We have open models with Kimi and GLM and others. I think the Western world is very hungry for additional open models that are Western open models, and so I believe that will happen over time as well. I think that the size of the opportunity in Bedrock is gigantic, and it could be a service as large as EC2, which is a very large service today in AWS. So I think it's very large. On the balance of chips and what you sell externally versus what you use inside your cloud, it's a very good question, and it's a question that we're continuing to evaluate as we speak. I would say that the number of companies who have a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. So there really aren't many customers that have to grapple with the same type of problem at this type of scale. At this point, everybody is producing their advanced chips with the same provider. There's only so many chips that provider can provide each year. Everybody gets an allocation. You have to decide with that allocation how much of it you want to sell externally and how much of it you want to use in your cloud. There's a trade-off. If you sell externally, you are able to realize more revenue in the short

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: term because you get to recognize the revenue as soon as it leaves your inventory. On the flip side, if you decide to use it inside your cloud in the form of EC2 instances or Bedrock, you actually will end up driving more absolute revenue and free cash flow from those chips because you get to use them over five to six years and drive revenue for a longer period of time. You have to really think through what you want to do. To date, I would say that we have taken a different approach in how we have used our chips than the other provider who has this same type of balancing act going on. As I mentioned earlier, we believe we are going to have a very significant business selling chips externally, and we are going to start in late 2027. We will be thinking through that balance, I think, probably every year. They will both be very significant. Our ability to create price-performance, scalable chips is going to be a very significant strategic advantage for us at scale, both in our own cost structure as well as in building a separate business and selling external chips. Selling external chips really is a very different business than your cloud infrastructure business.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Doug Anmuth with JPMorgan. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Doug Anmuth, Analyst
passages.text: Doug Anmuth, Analyst: Thanks for taking questions. When you think about the 40%+ AWS revenue growth each of the next two years and then the multi-year path beyond that, can you just talk about the CapEx required to drive that kind of revenue over the next couple of years and beyond? Also, Andy, any updates on how you are thinking about the duration of returns on both servers and networking and then also data centers? Thanks.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: Yeah. I'll take them in reverse order. On the break-even on our infrastructure, as I mentioned in my opening comments, we're continuing to move that left. We're continuing to make that shorter. There are a lot of cores, a little bit different from AI; it's a little bit different from how you finance these things. It varies depending on which you're talking about. But we're continuing to make progress, as we historically have been pretty good at doing, if you think about AWS, at finding ways to extend useful lives and to make the break-even sooner. We're making good progress there too. On the CapEx involved to grow the way we're talking about, it's meaningful. I think that the way we think about it, Doug, is that this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. I think what we're seeing with AI, it's the biggest transformation in our lifetime. If the idea of being able to grow 39% with a $184 billion annual run rate and to grow 40% a year on top of that in each of the next two years, and ultimately end up as a trillion-dollar-plus business, we're going to invest to continue being the leader. We are the leader today in the, I'll call it, the infrastructure and AI space. Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that's not the world that we live in, and that's not the opportunity. We can fund this plan. I think it will forever

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue, it will forever change our free cash flow, and we're going to invest, and we're going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thank you. Our final question comes from the line of Ross Sandler with Barclays. Please proceed with your question.

passages.heading: Ross Sandler, Analyst
passages.text: Ross Sandler, Analyst: Great. Yeah, I thought I would double down on the Bedrock question. The token marketplace on Bedrock seems to be one of the hottest services in AI right now. Our understanding is the majority of these workloads are running on Trainium. As this becomes a bigger part of the overall AWS story, like you just mentioned, Andy, how might that impact both revenue growth, but especially margins at AWS as you kind of shift from selling bare metal to selling more inference as a service? Could you just talk about that? Thank you.

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: Andy Jassy, CEO: Yeah. Well, you are right that the majority, and most of Bedrock today, is being run on top of Trainium. We do that in meaningful part because we really like the price performance that we are getting, and it allows us to both keep prices as low as possible for customers, as well as our ability—we like the margins associated with it. If you think about margins in the cloud space and you are looking at different players and what their cost structure looks like, there are a few things to pay attention to. The first is, for their data centers, how many of them are they actually buying or long-leasing versus doing colo or neoclouds? Neoclouds are about 3,500 basis points worse in operating margin than if you long-lease them. Then you look at what is the hardware on top of which they are running, and if you are using the hardware that everybody else is using, you will have a comparable cost structure to what everybody is doing. If you have the ability to use hardware that is different, you will have an advantage. I think when you look at what we are doing, most of our capacity is either owned or long-leased, which enjoys better operating margins than what you will find when people are mostly doing colo or neo, or a big chunk doing colo or neo. The fact that we are running on top of our own chip that is providing both an advantage in price performance and is more cost-effective for ourselves because we own it, I think gives us some structural cost advantages that I

passages.heading: Andy Jassy, CEO
passages.text: think are going to be very helpful to customers as we pass them back to customers and helpful to the overall economics of AWS.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Thanks for joining us for the call today and for your questions. A replay will be available on our investor relations website for at least three months. We appreciate your interest in Amazon and look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

# OpenAI IPO Valuation Target Reportedly Trimmed By $150B After Nasdaq 100 Registers Worst Month Since March 2025 Following Brutal Tech Sell-Off

Stocktwits News Desk

4 min read

* [OPAI.PVT](/quote/OPAI.PVT/ "OPAI.PVT")
* [^IXIC

  -2.86%](/quote/%5EIXIC/ "^IXIC")

* OpenAI had been seeking to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, after pointing to a sharp increase in revenue since July to justify nearly doubling its valuation from $852 billion.
* The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5% Friday, while the index registered its worst month since March 2025, adding pressure to companies tied to the AI trade.
* The report added that one OpenAI backer said that the fundraising process had begun amid enthusiasm for AI but was caught by a sharp reversal in the market.

OpenAI has reportedly cut its target for its latest funding round by $10 billion as the ChatGPT maker faces a tougher market backdrop and growing investor scrutiny of AI spending.

passages.heading: 9. [Investing](https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/investing/)
passages.text:
According to a report by The Financial Times citing people familiar with the matter, OpenAI is now seeking about $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, down from its earlier target of $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

[See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox](https://stocktwits.com/newsletters)

## OpenAI Tempers Ambitions

OpenAI had been seeking to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, after pointing to a sharp increase in revenue since July to justify nearly doubling its valuation from $852 billion.

But the company has since tempered its ambitions, with the report stating that OpenAI had set Friday as the deadline for investors to commit to the round. The initial close was expected to bring in less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, according to the report.

A consortium of investment groups from the United Arab Emirates, including state-backed technology fund MGX, is expected to be the largest participant. As part of the deal, OpenAI would have an option to lease newly developed computing power in the region, according to the report.

Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, along with SoftBank, also plan to participate, the report said. OpenAI raised $122 billion in March.

## Tech Sell-Off Puts AI Spending Under The Microscope

passages.heading: 9. [Investing](https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/investing/)
passages.text:
The fundraising reset comes after a sharp sell-off in technology stocks and growing concerns about the pace and scale of AI spending.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5% Friday, while the index registered its worst month since March 2025, adding pressure to companies tied to the AI trade. The Nasdaq 100 index closed lower by 6.65% in October, its worst month since March 2025 when it fell 7.69%.

The report added that one OpenAI backer said that the fundraising process had begun amid enthusiasm for AI but was caught by a sharp reversal in the market.

The company is also facing competition for investor attention from Anthropic, which is preparing for an IPO next month at a valuation of $1.5 trillion or more.

## Ives, Damodaran Weigh In On Anthropic IPO Risks

The Anthropic IPO could add another complication for OpenAI as investors weigh the two AI companies at the same time.

During an interview with CNBC, Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives described the [environment around Anthropic](https://stocktwits.com/news-articles/markets/equity/dan-ives-aswath-damodaran-anthropic-ipo-warning-credit-rating/cZUKHu7R9cZ) as a "perfect storm moment," saying the company is "so key to this AI revolution build out."

Ives continued to see a potential $1.5 trillion valuation for Anthropic despite the concerns. However, he acknowledged that Anthropic's fundraising needs could put it "a bit in the penalty box" as AI companies compete for capital to fund infrastructure.

passages.heading: 9. [Investing](https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/investing/)
passages.text:
NYU Stern professor Aswath Damodaran focused on the market mood heading into the IPO.

"IPOs are all about mood and momentum," Damodaran said, warning that the current environment could hurt Anthropic's initial reception. He also described Anthropic, OpenAI and other parts of the AI ecosystem as deeply interconnected.

"They're all connected at the hip. If one falls, they drag the others down with them," Damodaran warned.

During the after-hours session on Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, declined 1.77%; the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (QQQ) fell 3.47%; and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) closed lower by 1.07%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits toward the S&P 500 ETF was in the 'bullish' territory at the time of writing.

# ChatGPT Maker OpenAI Reportedly Cuts Funding Target to $20B

・

[버섯돌이(Taehyun Kim)](https://en.wowtale.net/author/mushman/)

[![](https://cdn.wowtale.net/wp-content/plugins/pavo-social-sharing/components/social-sharing/assets/icons/set6/facebook.svg)](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F11%2F01%2F235804%2F "Sharing on Facebook") [![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://twitter.com/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F11%2F01%2F235804%2F&text=ChatGPT+Maker+OpenAI+Reportedly+Cuts+Funding+Target+to+%2420B "Sharing on twitter") [![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](javascript:sendTalkLink( "Sharing on Kakao talk") [![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://line.me/R/msg/text/?ChatGPT Maker OpenAI Reportedly Cuts Funding Target to $20B%0D%0Ahttps://en.wowtale.net/2026/11/01/235804/ "Sharing on Line") [![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://www.band.us/plugin/share?body=ChatGPT+Maker+OpenAI+Reportedly+Cuts+Funding+Target+to+%2420B | https%3A%2F%2Fen.wowtale.net%2F2026%2F11%2F01%2F235804%2F "Sharing on Band") [![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='0'%20height='0'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](mailto:?subject=ChatGPT

Investor appetite for AI megadeals is cooling.

Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740 billion in capital spending this year, and Wall Street is [growing uneasy about negative free cash flow, mounting debt and the returns on all that spending](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/cracks-are-emerging-in-the-ai-spending-boom/).

Against that backdrop, the latest funding round for [OpenAI](http://en.wowtale.net/tag/openai), the maker of ChatGPT, is reportedly falling short. The Financial Times [reported on October 30](https://www.ft.com/content/7a3ad950-1b3b-4d9e-8c15-65a61ae6180f?syn-25a6b1a6=1) that OpenAI has lowered its target from $30 billion to $20 billion, with a first close expected to come in below that figure. A group of investors from the United Arab Emirates is set to lead the round, and a later retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total up to $20 billion.

The Wall Street Journal [followed up](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-raises-less-than-half-of-30-billion-target-in-latest-round-91aecdc5?st=pgo9cE&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink) with more detail: OpenAI has secured about $11 billion so far, and some large investors responded with tepid interest. The round values OpenAI at $1.25 trillion, below the $1.4 trillion it first sought. TechCrunch has asked OpenAI for comment.

## Expectations lowered twice in a month

Bloomberg first reported on September 29 that OpenAI was [seeking $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/29/openai-reportedly-in-talks-to-raise-30b-round-at-1-4t-valuation/), the [funding talks](https://en.wowtale.net/2026/10/02/235355/) Wowtale noted at the time. On October 22, CNBC [reported](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/openai-funding-round-uae-investors.html) that the valuation had been adjusted to $1.25 trillion, with [Coatue](https://www.coatue.com/) and UAE investors leading. The UAE money could also be paired with a deal for more computing capacity. OpenAI declined to comment.

The gap looks starker against OpenAI’s previous round. In February the company [announced $110 billion](https://techcrunch.com/2026/02/27/openai-raises-110b-in-one-of-the-largest-private-funding-rounds-in-history/) from [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/), [SoftBank Group](https://group.softbank/en) and [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com/) at a $730 billion pre-money valuation. The round later grew to $122 billion and closed at an [$852 billion post-money valuation](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/31/openai-not-yet-public-raises-3b-from-retail-investors-in-monster-122b-fund-raise/). In June OpenAI [filed confidentially for an IPO](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/08/following-anthropic-openai-files-confidentially-for-ipo/), so the price tag on this round also sets the bar for its eventual listing.

## Why Wall Street is jittery

Big Tech earnings explain the mood. Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second straight quarter in the red, as quarterly capex rose to $51.4 billion. Its stock fell 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record. Amazon’s trailing 12-month free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, and Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter. Microsoft was the exception, with $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow. The Nasdaq fell 2.9% on Friday.

The money is also coming from different places. According to [S&P Global Market Intelligence](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/29/ai-hyperscalers-stock-debt), Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle have raised a combined $326 billion in debt this year, triple last year’s total. For AI labs that depend on outside capital, that shift in sentiment is a direct headwind.

## Rival Anthropic faces its own test

OpenAI’s closest rival, [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), [raised $65 billion in a Series H in May at a $965 billion post-money valuation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/series-h), overtaking OpenAI’s $852 billion to become the world’s most valuable private AI company. Samsung and SK hynix took part. Anthropic had been valued at $380 billion in February, after [raising $30 billion](https://gvwire.com/?p=249698). A close at $1.25 trillion would put OpenAI back in front.

Anthropic [filed publicly for its IPO](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/26/anthropic-officially-files-for-its-public-debut/) on October 26, and Wowtale [dissected the S-1](https://en.wowtale.net/2026/10/27/235732/). CNBC has reported that it is eyeing a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion at listing. There is a catch, though. The FT reported that [Blackstone has warned investors](https://www.ft.com/content/59383c7f-8d82-493f-bf01-d2e862a1018f?syn-25a6b1a6=1) that Anthropic may not earn an investment-grade rating after its IPO, which would leave it more reliant on hyperscalers and third parties to fund its infrastructure.

Amazon said AWS revenue jumped 39.3% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in nearly five years, and guided for more than 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028 while projecting the cloud unit could reach $1 trillion in annual sales within five to 10 years. Backlog rose to $578 billion. The expansion is being funded by about $220 billion of 2026 capital spending, pushing trailing 12-month free cash flow to a $42.4 billion outflow. Total revenue of $201.94 billion and EPS of $1.89 missed estimates, and shares fell sharply. Analysts split between those backing the spending as necessary and those wary of valuation and retail softness.

##### Key Elements

![Amazon's AWS Backlog Hits $578 Billion as Jassy Maps Out a $1 Trillion Cloud Future](https://img.biggo.com/cpP90-QRx4L5ARCuLERMm8pm-D2kyZ0j56Aa7oZ7UvY/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2VmNjgxZjBmLWFlMzgtNDgxYy1iN2NmLTY0OWRkY2FkNzliM18xNzkzNDMwNDc5X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp)

Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) told investors this week that its cloud unit will keep expanding at more than 40% a year through 2028 and could eventually become a $1 trillion annual business, a stretch of guidance the company has rarely offered. The forecast came alongside third-quarter results that showed AWS growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years, but also a cash-flow picture that has turned sharply negative as the company pours money into AI infrastructure.

AWS revenue rose 39.3% to $46 billion in the quarter ended Sept. 30, the sixth consecutive quarter of accelerating growth and the quickest since late 2021. That lifted the unit's annualized run rate to $184 billion, while operating income climbed about 55% to $17.8 billion. Contracted work not yet booked as revenue, known as backlog, reached $578 billion, up from $496 billion at the end of the prior quarter.

On the earnings call, Chief Executive Andy Jassy said Amazon is installing an AI accelerator roughly every 14 seconds and that newly added capacity is being consumed almost as soon as it comes online. He expects AWS to grow faster than 40% in both 2027 and 2028 and wants to build the division into a $1 trillion-a-year operation within five to 10 years. Amazon also plans to start selling its in-house Trainium chips to customers outside AWS late in 2027.

#### The bill comes due

The growth has been financed with an extraordinary burst of spending. Amazon spent $77.3 billion on property and equipment in the quarter, up from $35.1 billion a year earlier, and reiterated plans for about $220 billion in cash capital expenditure for 2026. Jassy said outlays will be "meaningfully more" next year. Trailing 12-month free cash flow swung to an outflow of $42.4 billion from an inflow of $14.8 billion a year earlier, a shift the company attributed mainly to higher purchases of property and equipment tied to AI.

| Amazon Q3 2026 (vs. year earlier) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Total revenue | $201.94 billion, up 12% |
| Earnings per share | $1.89 |
| AWS revenue | $46 billion, up 39.3% |
| AWS operating income | $17.8 billion, up about 55% |
| AWS backlog | $578 billion |
| Quarterly capex (property and equipment) | $77.3 billion |
| Trailing 12-month free cash flow | -$42.4 billion |
| Q4 revenue guidance | $240 billion to $247 billion |

Note: Revenue and EPS fell short of analyst consensus of $202.31 billion and $1.97, respectively, according to FactSet-tracked estimates cited in press reports. The fourth-quarter guidance midpoint of $243.5 billion was also below the roughly $244.5 billion analysts had modeled.

Shares fell 4.25% on Oct. 29 ahead of the release and dropped more than 7% in after-hours and premarket trading as investors digested the spending plans and a softer holiday-quarter outlook. The stock closed down more than 1% on Friday, a milder decline than the rout that hit Alphabet after it reported a negative $9.1 billion in free cash flow and saw its shares fall 12.64% in a single session.

#### Two years of visibility

Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster argued in a note that the length of the guidance matters more than the headline growth number. Amazon typically gives only one quarter of AWS guidance, he wrote, so offering visibility into two full years signals confidence in AI demand that the company has seldom communicated so far in advance. He calculated that hitting $1 trillion in five years would require average annual growth of roughly 42%, and said AWS could account for about half of Amazon's total revenue within that window, up from roughly 21% today.

"Despite all of the hype, we are just starting," Munster wrote, calling the AI buildout a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

Wall Street's price targets moved in both directions. JPMorgan's Doug Anmuth kept an Overweight rating and a $365 target, nearly 50% above the pre-earnings close of $243.79, based on 26.5 times his 2028 earnings estimate. He pointed to custom chips and the Bedrock model platform as additional growth engines. Bank of America Securities' Justin Post maintained a Buy rating but trimmed his target to $317 from $320 while raising his 2027 revenue estimate to $968 billion and his 2027 capex forecast to $310 billion. KeyBanc's Justin Patterson cut his target to $345 from $350, and Cantor Fitzgerald's Deepak Mathivanan lowered his to $280 from $310.

The most cautious voice was D.A. Davidson's Gil Luria, who kept a Neutral rating and a $250 target, saying that while AWS acceleration is encouraging, elevated expectations and slower retail growth justify a balanced stance. Citizens' Andrew Boone cut his target to $275 from $315.

#### Beyond the cloud

The quarter's weakness was concentrated outside AWS. North American sales rose 6% to $112.85 billion and international revenue climbed 5% to $43.07 billion, with Amazon attributing part of the slowdown to a calendar shift that moved Prime Day into the second quarter in most major markets. Advertising growth decelerated to 12% from more than 20% in prior periods, though management expects a rebound to near 20% in the fourth quarter. Consolidated operating margin nonetheless reached a record 13.9%.

On the AI side, Amazon said Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock jumped nearly sevenfold year over year and total token volume on the platform rose about 17 times. Revenue commitments for Trainium and Graviton chips grew more than 20-fold, and Amazon says customers using its own silicon saved over $2 billion in the quarter. Jassy acknowledged a trade-off in selling Trainium externally: shipping chips generates revenue immediately, while keeping them inside AWS can produce more cumulative revenue and cash flow over the five to six years the hardware stays in service.

"We believe we're going to have a very significant business selling chips externally," he said.

The central question for investors now is whether the capacity being financed today converts into paying workloads fast enough to repair cash generation. Amazon says servers and networking gear pay back in under three years, while data centers have much longer useful lives. With free cash flow deeply negative and capex still climbing, the next several quarters of AWS growth and backlog conversion will determine how the market prices the buildout.

## **1. 💻 Microsoft: Azure Breaks Away**

Microsoft’s Q1 FY27 revenue (September quarter) rose 19% Y/Y to $92.3 billion ($1.5 billion beat), while adjusted EPS grew 18% to $4.89 ($0.17 beat).

**Azure revenue accelerated to 48% growth**, from 43% in Q4, comfortably exceeding expectations. Shares jumped as strong cloud demand and better-than-expected cash generation eased concerns about AI spending.

Microsoft also introduced a new reporting structure, combining its cloud and enterprise software businesses into two main segments:

* **Agents and Infra**, which grew 25% to $76.8 billion.
* **Devices and Consumer** declined 3% to $15.5 billion.

Microsoft revamped its reporting segments just two years ago, so another reshuffle feels like overkill. The visual below breaks down revenue by product and service instead, which I find more comprehensive and insightful.

The AI investment cycle is beginning to show tangible returns:

* **Azure reached $33.2 billion in revenue**, with growth expected to accelerate further to 49%–50% in Q2. Demand continues to exceed available capacity.
* **OpenAI-related commercial revenue reached $10 billion**, representing roughly 11% of Microsoft’s total revenue, up from about 7% in FY26. This strengthens AI monetization but also highlights customer concentration.
* **Microsoft 365 commercial cloud grew 18%**, adding another AI monetization source through Copilot. Meanwhile, customers using consumption-based Copilot billing grew more than 75%.

**Cash CapEx more than doubled to $39.4 billion,** while total capital spending, including leases, reached $45.2 billion. Operating cash flow grew 29% to $58 billion. As a result, **free cash flow fell 27% to $18.6 billion**. Microsoft expects CapEx to exceed $50 billion next quarter and accelerate further in early calendar 2027.

Commercial RPO remained enormous at **$677 billion**, up 73% Y/Y but roughly flat sequentially. That backlog provides visibility, though OpenAI likely still accounts for a substantial portion.

Microsoft is showing that AI infrastructure spending can drive accelerating revenue and strong profitability at the same time. The challenge is sustaining those returns as spending rises further, particularly if demand from OpenAI or other large AI customers becomes less predictable.

---

## **2. 💊 Eli Lilly: Volume Machine**

Eli Lilly’s Q3 revenue surged 39% Y/Y to $24.4 billion ($1.8 billion beat), while adjusted EPS grew 7% to $7.48 ($0.87 beat). **Volume increased 53%**, more than offsetting a 15% decline in realized prices. Shares jumped more than 6% as Lilly raised its annual revenue outlook by an impressive $5.5 billion.

**Mounjaro** and **Zepbound** generated a combined **$16.1 billion**, representing 66% of total revenue:

* **Mounjaro grew 65% to $10.7 billion**, with international sales surging 93% to $5.7 billion despite lower prices, particularly in China.
* **Zepbound grew 49% to $5.35 billion**, benefiting from expanded US insurance coverage. More than 500,000 patients have enrolled in the new Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, with roughly 70% starting on a Lilly medicine.
* **Foundayo reached $184 million**, up from $98 million in Q2 but below the ~$231 million consensus. Lilly’s oral obesity pill is struggling to match the early adoption of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill.

*Source: [Fiscal.ai](https://fiscal.ai/?via=appeconomyarticles)*

The quarter also benefited from **$900 million in favorable adjustments and milestone payments**, including $410 million from Jardiance that will not recur. Meanwhile, retatrutide delivered positive head-to-head Phase 3 results against Ozempic, strengthening Lilly’s next-generation obesity pipeline ahead of a planned Q1 2027 FDA filing.

Lilly raised FY26 revenue guidance to $91–92 billion (from $85–87 billion), while underlying EPS expectations increased by $4.07 at the midpoint. However, $4.57 in acquired R&D charges more than offset that improvement, leaving reported adjusted EPS guidance slightly lower at $35.00–36.00.

Lilly’s GLP-1 franchise continues to grow despite falling prices, with expanding coverage creating a larger addressable market. The challenge is sustaining extraordinary volume growth while building a second generation of treatments that can defend its market leadership.

---

## **3. 📱Samsung: Sold Out Through 2027**

Samsung’s Q3 revenue surged 127% Y/Y to a record ₩195.3 trillion (~$146 billion), while **operating profit climbed nearly ninefold** to ₩107.4 trillion (~$80 billion), another record. Operating margin reached an extraordinary 55%, up from 52% in Q2. Yet shares fell more than 4% as earnings missed elevated expectations and investors questioned how much of the AI windfall would reach shareholders.

The divergence between Samsung’s businesses is becoming extreme:

* **Semiconductor revenue rose 15% Q/Q** to ₩147.1 trillion, while operating profit climbed to ₩106.5 trillion. The chip division now accounts for **99% of Samsung’s total operating profit**.
* **HBM4 sales more than tripled Q/Q**, as Samsung gains ground in next-generation AI memory. Management says 2027 capacity is already fully booked, with supply shortages expected to persist through 2028.
* **The consumer electronics business lost ₩0.8 trillion** as soaring memory prices squeezed profitability in smartphones, TVs, and appliances. The same shortage fueling record semiconductor profits is hurting Samsung’s other businesses.
