# Does the AI money add up?

Who is really paying for the AI build-out, whether it rests on a few frontier labs or a broad base of buyers, and whether the promises add up. Built from company filings and reported deals, with our read kept separate from the record.

Data as of 2026-10-30. Amounts in US dollars. 59 companies and funders with sourced money in and out; 156 sourced money flows between named parties.

## Our answer

Not a house of cards. The demand is real, but the riskiest part rests on one company: OpenAI needs $60 to 105 billion of new money by 2028 just to stay on plan.

The buildings are paid for mostly by four of the most profitable companies in the world. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta will spend roughly $700 billion on data centers and equipment in 2026, most of it from their own cash. If AI disappoints, they earn poor returns. They do not go bust. But their survival is not the same as the system's safety: they can cut building and push the losses onto developers, equipment makers and lenders without ever missing a payment.

The paying customers behind the rest are few. Two labs, OpenAI and Anthropic, have signed about $1.2 trillion of firm compute purchases, $1.35 trillion counting Anthropic's cancellable contracts, against roughly $115 to 135 billion of annual revenue. OpenAI was about 45 percent of Microsoft's contracted backlog at the end of 2025 and is roughly half of Oracle's today. Take those two labs out and most of the Oracle, neocloud and Stargate build has no signed buyer today. That is concentration of contracts, not of demand: behind the two labs sit more than 50 million paying ChatGPT subscribers, 9 million paying business users, and over 11,900 companies paying Anthropic $100,000 a year or more.

A lot of the money those labs spend came from their own suppliers. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have put about $93 billion into the labs and the neoclouds that buy their products, with up to $242 billion in total if every conditional amount is paid. The labs owe those same suppliers about $822 billion in return. That makes revenue look bigger at both ends and ties the suppliers' results to two private companies.

The weak points are the borrowers in the middle: Oracle, rated one notch above junk with negative free cash flow and $288 billion of signed leases; SoftBank, funding OpenAI with junk bonds, loans secured on its shares and a $40 billion bridge loan; CoreWeave, where interest eats about a quarter of revenue; and the project companies behind Stargate. Almost all of that risk traces to one question: can OpenAI pay its bills? Anthropic looks sturdier. It is cash-positive from operations, holds $132 billion of cash and is about to go public.

Use is broad. Spending is thin in the middle and heavy at the top. More than half of businesses on Ramp's payment platform now pay for some AI, but the median paying business spends about $16 per employee a month, while the top tenth spend about $800. Breadth is growing, and Microsoft says last quarter's backlog growth came from customers outside the big labs. It is still small next to the labs' contracts.

Does it add up? We tested it year by year. Anthropic largely passes on analysts' cost estimates: on its plan it builds cash, and even if revenue stalls at today's rate it still holds about $105 billion at the end of 2028. Only in the harshest case, a stall while paying its contracts at the heaviest rate analysts estimate, does it run down to about $18 billion and need its IPO money early in 2029. Its equipment leases could also call for cash earlier than its expenses show. OpenAI does not pass on its own: even on its own plan it needs about $60 to 105 billion of new money by the end of 2028, about $320 billion by 2030 if growth comes in at half the plan, and about $470 billion if revenue stalls. Most of its planned computing is already signed, and much of its other spending is staff and overhead that does not shrink with revenue. Needing that money is not the same as failing to get it: so far each OpenAI round has been bigger than the last. If OpenAI's growth stalls, the first losses land on Oracle, SoftBank, the neoclouds and their lenders, and on Nvidia through its guarantees. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta take write-downs, not existential hits.

What would change our read: OpenAI reaching its $70 billion year-end revenue target, or missing it; Oracle's credit rating; SoftBank refinancing its $40 billion bridge loan; Big Tech free cash flow in the fourth quarter; order books on the next big tech bond; and how Anthropic's IPO prices.

This section is exmxc's judgment. The record it rests on follows, with sources, and each section keeps the record and our read apart.

* Microsoft priced $25B of bonds in ten parts on October 29, 2026. [Microsoft via SEC EDGAR, 2026-10-29](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000789019/000119312526439794/d799291dfwp.htm "Primary source: Microsoft pricing term sheet (Form FWP) for $25B notes")
* China's big tech companies are expected to spend about $140B on capex in 2026, against more than $785B for the six biggest US cloud companies (Moody's). [TNGlobal, 2026-08-28](https://technode.global/2026/08/28/chinese-hyperscalers-ramp-up-ai-spending-but-trail-us-rivals-moodys/ "Press report: Chinese hyperscalers ramp up AI spending but trail US rivals: Moody's")

#### Our read

The build is not three or four companies. It is about eight serious builders, and the top four fund most of it from businesses that earned money long before AI: ads, cloud, software and retail.

But three of the four now spend more than their businesses bring in. Free cash flow, the cushion that made this safe, is negative at Amazon, Alphabet and Meta. Microsoft is the exception on paper, but a change in how it counts leases now keeps a growing share of its building out of capex, and it just sold $25 billion of bonds anyway. The gap is being filled with debt.

This is a US story. China's big tech companies spend about a sixth as much, and they too have moved to negative free cash flow and new share sales to keep up.

#### Our read

This is the narrow part. Outside the big four's own products, the paying demand for new AI capacity is mostly two labs, plus Meta renting overflow. Each lab's signed purchases are roughly twenty times those of the next buyer on the list, Meta.

The Microsoft data point matters and cuts the other way: new backlog from ordinary enterprise customers is real and growing. It is not yet big enough to replace a lab that stops paying.
